review: Independent freeze review of the first two-arm companion attempt (gate C5 only), before any paid call. Read-only: no paid model call, no API key read, no pytest, no service or database started, nothing pushed; the only file written is this one. No held-out content was read: scenario, findings and review files were only hashed, counted (line counts and grep -c pattern counts, never displayed) and passed to c5-precheck.py and freeze.py, which print counts and codes only.

findings.what: Each scenario rests on one fast full review, and the cheap extra check the kit seems to offer is not available. The launcher refuses a verifier on a version that has already been reviewed ('the current version was already reviewed or verified: a fixer comes first', launch.py around lines 314-322). An approving verifier would also rewrite control/KEY-review-approved.json, which is frozen in the manifest. So there is no kit path for a second reading of the frozen versions without a fixer making a new version.
findings.where: evaluations/acceptance-kit/launch.py (verifier preconditions, receipt writing at around lines 466-478); binding decision 10 and the limit 'Each scenario had one reviewer'
findings.why_it_matters: The precheck plus one Sonnet reading of about 70 s per scenario (05:03:12-05:04:22 and 05:10:55-05:12:02) is everything that stands behind the scenarios' wording. From outside the review looks complete: the message-scan section has 61 of 61 lines for c1 and 63 of 63 for c2, with 16 and 20 distinct session ids. Every scan line starts with 'ok', and each review has 2 minor findings and 0 blocking. That pace is the reviewer's normal pace: the public diagnostics' reviewers took 88 s (d2, which found a real F7 date error) and 90 s (d3, scenario-two items, 0 blocking). Nothing shows that the per-case checks (F2, F3, F4, F8) were made beyond these two minor findings. Most scenario defects would weaken both arms alike and so lower sensitivity, not tilt the result, and the real money at risk is small (about a sixth of the guard count). So I judge this enough to spend this ceiling on, but not enough to read a pass as strong evidence. Cheapest added assurance that keeps the scenarios sealed: one isolated Sonnet session per scenario with c5-verifier-brief.md (fatal classes over the whole file), run outside the round ledger, with its output written outside control/ so that no receipt changes and only approved/blocking counts reach the operator. The binding does not provide for that session, so it is a recorded deviation, or a binding addendum, which means a new commit, a new head, and redoing the manifest, preparation.json and this review, with the scenarios, receipts and persona unchanged. If that session finds a blocking instance, the scenario must be fixed. That makes a new scenario sha256 and needs a kit verification that rewrites the receipt. Then all of these must be frozen again: the manifest, both receipts as rewritten, preparation.json, the binding's scenario hashes, the production table, the novelty figures and precheck lines, and the statement that the persona was computed after both scenarios were final (now false for the fixed one), followed by a new freeze review.

findings.what: The cost estimate gives no upper bound and no decision point. Its basis, 0.232 CNY per scenario-turn, comes from runtime a85ca152. That runtime predates c280dcbf ('index before it replies') and 55a88f1f ('use memory tools before it writes its reply'), both of which change P's rounds per turn. The 25% uplift is unverified. The caps allow up to 4 host rounds per P turn (5 calls per turn over the arm, counting retries).
findings.why_it_matters: The seventh attempt made 327 requests for 248 arm-turns. If P now needs about 3 requests per turn at about 12k prompt tokens, the guard count nears the 59.945984 CNY refusal point during c2. That would stop the attempt with no C5 result and nothing retried. The script runs c2 without any decision point after c1. The run can still be started, but the operator should know this risk (see conditions).

findings.what: The two new refusals check only that control/owner-approval.json and control/provider-revalidation.json parse as JSON objects. A revalidation that records a mismatch, or an empty {}, passes. balance.py exits 0 on any HTTP 200, whatever is_available says and however low the balance is.
findings.why_it_matters: The binding says that a revalidation mismatch stops the attempt before any call. The script does not enforce this: the lead's procedure does. An insufficient balance would make the first host request fail with a non-2xx status. The guard would then block the ledger, so no money would be lost, but the attempt would be consumed, because a stopped ledger is never reopened.

findings.what: The binding gives no way to stop a running attempt. Started with setsid, the script, the driver and the harness share one session. Killing run-live.sh or its process group skips the script's step 6: execution-done, the final balance, the cleanup of each run directory and the port check.
findings.where: binding, Running the attempt; run-live.sh (no trap)
findings.why_it_matters: An operator who has to stop the run early, for example on a cost forecast or a hang, could leave services running and records incomplete. The safe way follows from the driver's documented signal handling: send SIGTERM to the driver's PID only. The driver forwards it to the runner's supervisor, which blocks the ledger, and run-live.sh then carries out step 6.

findings.what: The binding says the two new refusals come 'before anything else'. In the script they come after the head, clean-tree, manifest and freeze-review checks, and before the port, disk, ledger and runs checks.
findings.where: binding, Running the attempt, second bullet of the changes
findings.why_it_matters: This is wording only; the order in the script is sound. The block is byte-identical to run-live.sh (sha256 d0655f20...c251), so the code governs.

findings.what: The 'Limits a C5 result will have' list, which the record must state whatever the result, leaves out a limit that decision 7 states: R4 passed on runtime a85ca152, older than this pin, so the R4 result and a C5 result on ef0e8727 do not together qualify one release runtime.
findings.where: binding, decision 7 against the Limits section
findings.why_it_matters: A record written from the Limits list alone could suggest that R4 and C5 now hold for one runtime.

findings.what: The frozen policy file still carries the labels "status": "draft_not_approved" and "for": "sixth maturity attempt: R4 only". The binding reuses it unchanged for C5, as the seventh attempt did.
findings.why_it_matters: The approval lives only in control/owner-approval.json, which the script does not read. That record should name the policy hash and the 80 CNY ceiling explicitly, so that the file's own label cannot be cited against the run.

findings.what: The list of host behaviours that can still end a run as invalid matches the code as far as I could read it, with one theoretical gap. A turn's last round offers no tools (after three tool rounds or six calls). If the host answers that round with tool calls and no text, the reply is empty and validity refuses the run ('empty reply'). Host.call retries an empty reply only when there are no tool calls. Separately, a 4xx from the provider on such a tools-less request, which carries tool history, would stop the attempt as a provider failure.
findings.where: c5-harness.py lines 1617-1650 (the turn loop) and Host.call
findings.why_it_matters: This is unlikely with an OpenAI-compatible API, but neither the binding nor c5-harness.md names it, and the attempt has no retry.

Each scenario's wording rests on one Sonnet review of about 70 s, with no verification round. The review procedure's later rounds would not be independent of round 1 anyway. The criteria templates fix every coverage case's 'must' and 'must not'.
Partial blinding with two arms: memory remarks can reveal the arm, and the remark count undercounts.

F has no memory layers. It learns page boundaries, resets, clearing, support style, familiarity limit and mood pin from one fixed line, and is told about resets while P's host is not (this tilts reset cases toward F). F's critical errors bound P's host-caused allowance.
Host labelling decides type 6. A host step that fails still counts as a fail: the result is for memBrain together with this host under emulation.

Persona cases are judged against what the user asked for and agreed to. 'From now on' yeses are only in the same conversation. The persona-version list says only 'in the conversation' for changes made by tool.
not_applicable page actions are scored but leave their item unexercised. C1 has 1 page action and C2 has 3, so a single missing host step can leave an item untested while the gate still passes.
No off-the-record stretch, so pause on the user's words, resume and honesty about an unrecorded stretch are not exercised.
R4 passed on runtime a85ca152. This C5 runs on ef0e8727 code (clone src identical), so the two results do not qualify one release runtime together.
The attempt is single-shot. Any provider or transport error (including a reply slower than the 600 s client timeout) blocks the ledger and ends it with no retry, across about 400-550 paid requests.
The guard count is conservative (no cache discount). The real bill was about a sixth of it in the seventh attempt, but the guard count is what can stop the run.
